article_html:
Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, winning a reprieve for the polarising Pentagon chief ​before Democrats take control of Congress next year and possibly try again.

The vote on a procedural motion came just hours after Hegseth blasted efforts to impeach him as ‌a farce and delivered a defiant defence of his record at the helm of the US military, winning praise from President Donald Trump.

The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favour of a motion to refer eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, a move that the sponsor of the impeachment push, US Representative Thomas Massie, warned would kill it.

Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth’s policies and wary of the unpopularity ​of the eight-month-old Iran war, but no other Republicans joined him.

The US-Israeli-led conflict has never been approved by Congress, which is the only branch of government constitutionally permitted to ​declare war.

Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment articles, which accuse Hegseth of the “high crimes and misdemeanours” of illegally ordering the military to wage war ⁠in Iran and Yemen, attack boats in the Caribbean Sea and abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January.

But 11 Democrats, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, did not vote.

If eight of ​them had, the procedural measure would have been defeated, paving the way for a full House impeachment vote.

Ian Krager, a spokesperson for Pelosi, said she had missed the vote because she had returned to San Francisco ​for an annual event to honour veterans, but would have voted against the procedural measure.

Trump cheered the results in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth “has miserably FAILED!”

He wrote that Hegseth’s performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”

Hegseth would have been the first US defence secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the ​title “secretary of war.”

Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when he took office last year.

Trump cannot change the name of the ​Defence Department without approval from Congress.

Iran war anger

Voter anger over the Iran war, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos ‌poll published ⁠on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress, which takes office in January, to act to end the war with Iran once and for all.

Although Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and blamed it for the Republicans’ midterm rout, he voiced support for Hegseth on Tuesday.

“This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” Vance wrote on social media.

Before the vote, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday: “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war ​of choice in Iran.”

Hegseth has repeatedly defended the ​conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran’s military ⁠has been left in ruins.

He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie’s accusations of “high crimes and misdemeanours”.

“History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now,” Hegseth said on Tuesday at his first Pentagon briefing in six months.

Jeffries said he would talk to ​members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

A Democratic-led push to ​impeach Hegseth could be far ⁠more intense, with lawmakers calling in top brass to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far.

Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy’s top admiral, a woman, among others.

In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues of concern to voters, including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the US ⁠military’s strikes on ​suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.

Some Republicans say Hegseth’s strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability ​as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military’s budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion.

Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.

“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay ​on board,” he said.

headline: Americans want new Congress to end Iran war, repeal Trump tariffs
description: Reuters/Ipsos poll finds 71% back legislation to end conflict, while 62% support repealing import tariffs
author: Reuters
article_text:
Majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end ​the war with Iran and to repeal tariffs put in place by President Donald Trump, signalling demand for quick action to address ‌the high cost of living, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The four-day poll, completed on Monday, showed 71% of Americans – including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans – want the US Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict with Iran that Trump launched alongside US ally Israel in February.

Democrats won their largest majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives since at least 2008 ​in last week’s midterm elections, in a sharp rebuke to Trump’s Republicans over high costs and a deeply unpopular war.

Democrats will take ​power when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

A smaller but still-significant share of respondents – 62% – said ⁠they would support an effort to repeal tariffs on imports put in place by the Trump administration.

The war with Iran has pushed fuel prices sharply ​higher, adding to inflation already stoked by the new taxes Trump slapped on hundreds of imported goods.

Trump has defended the war as necessary to prevent Iran ​from acquiring a nuclear weapon. The tariffs, he has said, will boost American industry by protecting it from cheap imports.

Democratic Party leaders have vowed to address cost-of-living concerns and say they will try to force an end to the US war with Iran. Many in the party have also vowed to end Trump’s tariffs.

Desire for bipartisanship

Large majorities ​of people in both political parties said it was important for Trump to make an effort to work with Democrats and for Democratic leaders in the ​new Congress to try to work with the president.

Nine in 10 respondents said cost of living issues should be a focus for the Congress during its first 100 days.

Smaller ‌shares wanted ⁠a focus on issues like artificial intelligence regulation, immigration reform and climate change.

Opposition to impeachment

But many Americans appear concerned Democrats will use their new power to launch legal proceedings against Trump. Some 42% of poll respondents said it would be “bad for the country” if the new Congress tried to impeach Trump, compared with 33% who said it would be good for the country. The rest weren’t sure or didn’t answer the question.

Congressional Democrats are divided on how to bring down ​healthcare costs, and also disagree on ​how aggressively to target Trump, including ⁠whether to impeach the president or members of his cabinet.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to face a House impeachment vote this week, following a move by a Republican lawmaker.

While Trump said after the elections he would “probably” get along with ​Democrats, he also promoted Stephen Miller, a polarising aide who has called the Democratic Party a domestic extremist group, ​to be his new ⁠White House chief of staff.

While the poll showed Trump’s approval rating near the lowest level of his political career, at 32%, it also showed Democrats were not particularly popular either.

Some 45% of Americans had a favourable view of Democrats, while 51% had an unfavourable view. Some 35% had a favourable view of Republicans, and 60% viewed them unfavourably.

Asked ⁠which party ​had a better approach to regulating artificial intelligence, which could be an important issue for Congress ​in the coming months, 28% picked Democrats, and 20% picked Republicans, while the rest said they weren’t sure or that neither was better.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from ​1,705 US adults and had a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

headline: Trump administration moves to cut food stamps for 6.3 million people
description: Proposed SNAP changes could also affect free school meals for 1.8 million children
author: Reuters
article_text:
The Trump administration ‌on Tuesday moved to cut millions more Americans from the nation’s largest food assistance program, even as enrollment continues to fall from other administration cuts.

A proposed rule issued by the US Department ​of Agriculture would curb automatic eligibility for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, ​also known as food stamps, for households receiving cash aid under ⁠the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families Program.

Currently, households receiving TANF benefits qualify for ​SNAP without needing to meet federal income thresholds. TANF eligibility varies by state but ​is generally 130% to 200% of the federal poverty level. SNAP eligibility is generally 130% of the federal poverty level.

Under the USDA’s proposed change, nearly 18% of SNAP recipients, or about 6.3 ​million people, would lose benefits, according to an agency analysis included in the ​proposed rule.

The changes would make SNAP eligibility more standardised and “preserve benefits for the truly needy,” the ‌rule ⁠said.

More than 5.5 million people have already lost SNAP benefits since President Donald Trump enacted cuts to the program in his July 2025 tax law, bringing enrollment to about 36 million people, according to USDA data.

The enrollment decline is partly due to ​struggles by states ​to implement administrative ⁠changes to the program and also to absorb high new costs from Trump’s law.

Because SNAP enrollment also confers eligibility for other food ​aid programs, the USDA estimates that 1.8 million children would ​also lose ⁠eligibility for free school lunch under its proposed rule.

Democratic Representative Angie Craig of Minnesota, ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, in a statement called the rule “heartless and ⁠cruel.”

“The proposed ​rule would make it harder to meet basic ​needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs,” she said.

The public will have 30 days to ​comment on the proposed rule.

headline: Israel's parliament sworn in as Eisenkot tries to forge a govt
description: Gadi Eisenkot faces difficult task of building a coalition while prospect of fresh vote looms
author: Reuters
article_text:
Israel’s parliament was sworn in on Tuesday without a new ​government, after a deadlocked general election stripped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his parliamentary majority but left his main rivals with no clear path ‌to power.

Lawmakers elected in the October 27 vote took their oaths of office as Gadi Eisenkot, a former general, sought to forge a coalition after Israel’s president tasked him on Sunday with forming a government.

Eisenkot and his allies also lack a majority, and he has yet to strike deals with parties that could bring him to power.

If both Eisenkot and Netanyahu fail to form coalitions, another ​election could follow.

Presiding over the swearing-in ceremony, President Isaac Herzog told lawmakers: “You must do everything to avoid a repeat election.”

“Reach out a hand for compromise, ​even between rivals… Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability ⁠and experience found in every part of this House.”

October 7 inquiry

Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until a new candidate manages to ​form a coalition.

His radical Likud party’s alliance with extremist and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority, now holding 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.

Eisenkot’s ​centre-right Yashar party and patchwork partner factions hold just 48 seats.

But they have potential allies in Israel’s Arab-led parties, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.

This means that the newly sworn-in parliament could still deliver on some of Eisenkot’s campaign promises, such as potentially setting up a commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023 ​attacks, something backed by the Arab parties but largely opposed by Netanyahu.

It also could allow Eisenkot to replace the current Knesset Speaker, a Likud member.

Herzog told Knesset members ​that parliament was “duty-bound to leave no stone unturned” in investigating and understanding the “catastrophe” of October 7, while Israel continues to face threats from Iran and its proxies.

Eisenkot initially has until December ‌6 to ⁠form a government, but he can seek a two-week extension to December 20.

He has acknowledged his path to power is “extraordinarily complex”.

His options include trying to form a minority government with Arab party support, bringing ultra-Orthodox parties into his camp despite years of mutual hostility, or forging a unity government with Netanyahu.

All three paths face formidable obstacles.

Ultra-Orthodox parties have so far said they would not join an Eisenkot-led government.

For his part, Netanyahu has cast doubt on the election results by baselessly alleging voter fraud by Arabs, who ​make up a fifth of the population. ​

Election officials have said they are ⁠probing potential misconduct, but that they have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the vote’s outcome.

Speaking after parliament was sworn in, Netanyahu called for a unity government, warning that Iran was seeking to revive its nuclear programme and that Israel ​could come under growing international pressure to accept a nuclear-armed Iran.

“Only such a (unity) government will be capable of confronting challenges ​of this magnitude,” he ⁠said.

If Eisenkot fails to form a government, Herzog would likely ask Netanyahu to try to build a coalition.

If he also fails, another candidate would get a chance before Israel would be forced into another election.

Moments after the official opening of parliament, Eisenkot and his allies submitted a series of bills, including legislation to establish a state commission of inquiry into ⁠the October ​7 attacks and to impose term limits on the prime minister.

They also proposed repealing a controversial ​judicial overhaul and other laws enacted under Netanyahu’s government over the past four years.

Among those sworn in on Tuesday was Elisha Madan, a military reservist who lost both legs fighting in Gaza.

He received a ​standing ovation from lawmakers as he rose on his prosthetic legs to take the oath of office.

headline: Actor Stacy Keach, best known as Mike Hammer, dies at 85
description: A veteran actor also won a Golden Globe for portraying novelist Ernest Hemingway in a television miniseries
author: Reuters
article_text:
Actor Stacy Keach, who portrayed rugged characters such as fictional detective Mike Hammer and legendary American novelist Ernest Hemingway, died on Tuesday at the age of 85, his wife said in a statement to Hollywood trade publication Variety.

Keach died in Poland “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure,” ​Malgosia Tomassi said in a statement to Variety.

“Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also ‌my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family,” Tomassi said.

Keach stood out in dozens of starring and character actor parts on television and in films in roles as diverse as Barabbas (the TV miniseries “Jesus of Nazareth”) and Richard Nixon (the play “Frost/Nixon”).

He also had a busy stage career, often starring in Shakespearean works such as “King Lear” and “Hamlet.”

His performance as the latter in 1972 inspired a New ​York Times critic to label Keach “the finest American classic actor since John Barrymore.”

Keach’s most prominent role was Mike Hammer, the hard-boiled detective, clad in a fedora and ​trenchcoat, in television adaptations of the works of suspense writer Mickey Spillane.

“The New Mike Hammer” ran from the mid to late 1980s ⁠, and Keach revived the character in the “Mike Hammer, Private Eye” series from 1997-98.

He also played Hammer in four made-for-television movies and narrated audio versions of Spillane’s books.

“I have ​been and always shall be Mike Hammer,” Keach wrote in his 2013 autobiography, “All in All: An Actor’s Life on and off the Stage.”

He added, “Certain roles stick to you, and I’m ​happy that Hammer is mine.”

The first Hammer series was interrupted when Keach went to prison for six months in England in 1985 after more than 30 grams of cocaine were found in his possessions at London’s Heathrow Airport.

In his book, he said he had been addicted, and in 2013 Keach told Fox News that getting caught “saved my life, actually.”

Keach had a history with Hemingway, the complex Nobel ​Prize-winning author and adventurer.

His portrayal of the writer in “Hemingway” in the 1988 television miniseries earned him a Golden Globe award and an Emmy nomination.

Keach was born June 2, ​1941, in Savannah, Georgia, and grew up in Southern California. As a child, he underwent several surgeries for a cleft lip and cleft palate.

“Only when I was maligned and teased by kids ‌did it bother ⁠me,” Keach told Fox News. “I became an overachiever as a result of that. I had to excel in sports to make up for that. It was a motor. It gave me an incentive to do better.”

For some roles, the scar on his lip was concealed by a moustache, but in a 2016 interview with the Cleft Palate Foundation, Keach said he preferred to let it show when he was in a tough-guy role, such as a mobster, or playing a vulnerable character.

Keach’s father, Stacy Sr., was a director and actor ​who worked steadily in television from the ​1950s through the ’80s. His brother James ⁠Keach was also an actor.

Keach graduated from the University of California at Berkeley and also studied at the Yale School of Drama and was a Fulbright Scholar at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

In the foreword of “All in All,” actor Alec Baldwin described ​Keach as “a miraculous hybrid of the hyper-masculinity of a Brando or Robert Mitchum and the classical training of Richard Burton or ​Kevin Kline.”

Keach’s movie work ⁠included John Huston’s “Fat City,” “The New Centurions,” “The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean,” “American History X,” “The Long Riders” with his brother, “That Championship Season,” and the Cheech and Chong comedies “Up in Smoke” and “Nice Dreams.”

His regular television roles included “Titus,” “Prison Break” and “Two and a Half Men.” On Broadway, he starred in “Other Desert Cities” in 2011-2012, “The Kentucky Cycle” and “Solitary Confinement” in the ’90s and “Deathtrap” in the ’70s.

Keach suffered an apparent ⁠heart attack ​on stage in May 2017 on opening night of “Pamplona,” a one-man play about Hemingway in his later ​years, that forced the cancellation of the show’s run.

He also suffered a mild stroke in 2009 during a run of “Frost/Nixon” but returned to the stage 10 days later.

Keach is survived by Tomassi, a Polish-born actress who ​appeared with him in various “Hammer” shows. He was married three times previously and had a years-long relationship with singer Judy Collins in the ’70s.

headline: Pakistani migrant among 112 foreigners died in Greek custody: Study
description: Researchers find over 100 deaths in police stations and migrant detention centres since 2000
author: Reuters
article_text:
More than 100 foreign nationals have died since 2000 ‌in Greek police stations or migrant centres with inadequate healthcare facilities, including 34 deaths that have not been officially registered, according to research published on Tuesday by Oxford University researchers.

In total, the research found ​112 deaths in the 26-year period, including 44 suicides.

Of the 112 deaths, ​84 occurred in police stations without medical staff, and 27 were reported ⁠in migrant detention facilities.

The Greek government and the police ministry did not immediately respond to ​a request for comment.

The dataset, part of an ongoing project that monitors deaths of foreign ​nationals in detention, including those held on criminal grounds, draws on police statistics obtained through freedom of information requests, international monitoring reports, media and testimonies.

The findings reveal “gaps in official police records and serious barriers ​to healthcare, including in facilities receiving EU funding,” the report’s authors said in a statement.

​They said 34 deaths documented by journalists, NGOs and monitors were not included in the police statistics.

The ‌data, ⁠published on the research platform Detention Landscapes, reflects complaints by human rights groups and follows a 2026 report by the Council of Europe’s anti-torture committee (CPT).

The report said that deaths in police custody in Greece had increased and some could have been prevented with sufficient supervision, ​psychiatric care and healthcare.

Among ​the cases it examined ⁠was the death of a 37-year-old Pakistani migrant while in detention at an Athens police station.

The CPT also cited persistent overcrowding in prison ​cells, including five people in spaces meant for one, and detainees ​sleeping on ⁠concrete or bedbug-infested mattresses.

Greece, long a landing point for migrants trying to enter the European Union from Africa, Asia and the Middle East, told the CPT that it was taking steps ⁠to address ​deficiencies under a 2025-2030 action plan to improve detention ​conditions, protect prisoners’ rights, boost staff and ease prison overcrowding, a problem in over 60% of countries worldwide, according ​to a 2024 UN report.

headline: India garment makers rethink reliance on US after tariff shock
description: Companies shift towards Europe and other markets to reduce reliance on Washington
author: Reuters
article_text:
At Orient Craft’s factory in Ranchi, hundreds of women stitch dresses, shirts and children’s clothing for British retailers ​Next and Marks & Spencer.

Not long ago, most of Orient Craft’s output would have gone to the US. But founder Sudhir Dhingra, 77, has cut shipments there since ‌the US hiked tariffs, which rose to as much as 50% last year, hitting orders from customers including American Eagle and Gap.

Even with duties now lower and the possibility of a trade pact, Dhingra has decided it is too much of a risk to depend so heavily on one market.

“Even if there is a deal, what is the guarantee that it will hold water?” he said. “I don’t wish to see that sword on my head.”

Orient ​Craft is one of many Indian companies reconfiguring their export destinations and their exposure to the US, in light of the tariff shock, in a move that is likely ​to strengthen New Delhi’s hand in its trade negotiations with Washington, and potentially reduce India’s vulnerability to US pressure over time.

Dhingra said US buyers ⁠cancelled orders or sought discounts after US President Donald Trump first announced the tariff hikes in April 2025, with some asking suppliers to absorb 25% of the duty, despite manufacturers’ margins being ​less than 10%.

Orient Craft has since moved sales to Britain, Europe and, to a lesser extent, India.

The US now accounts for less than 10% of sales, down from 84% before the ​tariffs, with annual exports of about 1.5 billion rupees ($15.82 million).

US duties on Indian products are currently 10% under Section 301, a US law allowing tariffs on imports, as well as base tariffs from 6% to 12%.

Gokaldas Exports, which employs more than 53,000 people and is one of India’s biggest garment exporters, is turning to Europe.

“It is not a temporary shift,” said Managing Director Sivaramkrishnan Ganapathi.

The company aims to raise Europe’s revenue share to 25% ​to 30% over the next 3 to 5 years, he said, from 15% to 16%, reducing the US share to 35% to 40% from 50% to 55%.

In April to August, ​India’s textile, apparel and home-furnishings exports to the US fell 9.8% to $4.0 billion, while shipments to other markets rose 3.7% to $15.2 billion, according to the Global Trade Research Institute.

The US share of Indian exports fell to ‌25.4% at ⁠the end of August from 28.3% in 2022, according to industry estimates.

Building new markets, lowering costs

Exporters said US tariff uncertainty, higher shipping costs and US buyers’ discount demands have squeezed margins, making other markets, including the UAE, UK and EU, look more attractive.

Indian clothing also gets duty-free access to Britain under the India-UK trade deal that came into effect in July, while a similar EU agreement could eliminate duties of 12% to 17%.

“Germany, France, Italy and the Netherlands are key targets,” said A. Sakthivel, chairman of the Apparel Export Promotion Council, an industry group.

Exporters are also looking to lower ​manufacturing costs.

Ranchi, in the eastern state of Jharkhand, ​is best known for coal and iron ⁠ore, but is now luring garment factories with subsidies, easier land access and its educated and reliable workforce.

Reuters visited three factories in and around Ranchi, together employing about 8,000 people.

“We have at least a 10% efficiency advantage here over other locations,” said Mrityunjay Singh, senior vice president of ​operations at Gokaldas, which has two factories in Ranchi and plans to open a third, creating up to 4,600 jobs.

“We can’t rely ​on a single market, product ⁠or buyer,” said Birendra Rawat of Ranchi-based Auburn Design, which makes Jockey underwear and clothing for local licensee Page Industries, and produces 5 million to 6 million garments a month to be sold in India and neighbouring countries.

India’s own apparel market, valued at $150 billion and growing 7% to 8% annually, provides a buffer against export uncertainty through steadier cash flows and demand.

“Diversification is becoming a structural strategy, especially ⁠for exporters heavily ​exposed to the US market,” said Chandrima Chatterjee, secretary general of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry.

Exporters said they ​would not abandon the US completely given the size of the market and longstanding relationships with buyers.

Still, the upheaval of the tariff shock meant it was unlikely to regain its former dominance, even if duties eased.

“The US market ​remains important, but it can’t decide the future of thousands of families who depend on us,” Dhingra said.

Not long ago, most of Orient Craft’s output would have gone to the US. But founder Sudhir Dhingra, 77, has cut shipments there since ‌the US hiked tariffs, which rose to as much as 50% last year, hitting orders from customers including American Eagle and Gap.

Even with duties now lower and the possibility of a trade pact, Dhingra has decided it is too much of a risk to depend so heavily on one market.

“Even if there is a deal, what is the guarantee that it will hold water?” he said. “I don’t wish to see that sword on my head.”

Orient ​Craft is one of many Indian companies reconfiguring their export destinations and their exposure to the US, in light of the tariff shock, in a move that is likely ​to strengthen New Delhi’s hand in its trade negotiations with Washington, and potentially reduce India’s vulnerability to US pressure over time.

Dhingra said US buyers ⁠cancelled orders or sought discounts after US President Donald Trump first announced the tariff hikes in April 2025, with some asking suppliers to absorb 25% of the duty, despite manufacturers’ margins being ​less than 10%.

Orient Craft has since moved sales to Britain, Europe and, to a lesser extent, India.

The US now accounts for less than 10% of sales, down from 84% before the ​tariffs, with annual exports of about 1.5 billion rupees ($15.82 million).

US duties on Indian products are currently 10% under Section 301, a US law allowing tariffs on imports, as well as base tariffs from 6% to 12%.

Gokaldas Exports, which employs more than 53,000 people and is one of India’s biggest garment exporters, is turning to Europe.

“It is not a temporary shift,” said Managing Director Sivaramkrishnan Ganapathi.

The company aims to raise Europe’s revenue share to 25% ​to 30% over the next 3 to 5 years, he said, from 15% to 16%, reducing the US share to 35% to 40% from 50% to 55%.

In April to August, ​India’s textile, apparel and home-furnishings exports to the US fell 9.8% to $4.0 billion, while shipments to other markets rose 3.7% to $15.2 billion, according to the Global Trade Research Institute.

The US share of Indian exports fell to ‌25.4% at ⁠the end of August from 28.3% in 2022, according to industry estimates.

Building new markets, lowering costs

Exporters said US tariff uncertainty, higher shipping costs and US buyers’ discount demands have squeezed margins, making other markets, including the UAE, UK and EU, look more attractive.

Indian clothing also gets duty-free access to Britain under the India-UK trade deal that came into effect in July, while a similar EU agreement could eliminate duties of 12% to 17%.

“Germany, France, Italy and the Netherlands are key targets,” said A. Sakthivel, chairman of the Apparel Export Promotion Council, an industry group.

Exporters are also looking to lower ​manufacturing costs.

Ranchi, in the eastern state of Jharkhand, ​is best known for coal and iron ⁠ore, but is now luring garment factories with subsidies, easier land access and its educated and reliable workforce.

Reuters visited three factories in and around Ranchi, together employing about 8,000 people.

“We have at least a 10% efficiency advantage here over other locations,” said Mrityunjay Singh, senior vice president of ​operations at Gokaldas, which has two factories in Ranchi and plans to open a third, creating up to 4,600 jobs.

“We can’t rely ​on a single market, product ⁠or buyer,” said Birendra Rawat of Ranchi-based Auburn Design, which makes Jockey underwear and clothing for local licensee Page Industries, and produces 5 million to 6 million garments a month to be sold in India and neighbouring countries.

India’s own apparel market, valued at $150 billion and growing 7% to 8% annually, provides a buffer against export uncertainty through steadier cash flows and demand.

“Diversification is becoming a structural strategy, especially ⁠for exporters heavily ​exposed to the US market,” said Chandrima Chatterjee, secretary general of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry.

Exporters said they ​would not abandon the US completely given the size of the market and longstanding relationships with buyers.

Still, the upheaval of the tariff shock meant it was unlikely to regain its former dominance, even if duties eased.

“The US market ​remains important, but it can’t decide the future of thousands of families who depend on us,” Dhingra said.

headline: Oil rises from two-month low as Hormuz shipping attacks offset Iran truce hopes
description: Oil rebounds as Hormuz attacks keep supply concerns alive
author: Reuters
article_text:
Oil prices rose on Wednesday after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Iran ​war and concerns about ongoing attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent ‌futures climbed 71 cents, or 0.78%, to $92.20 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 49 cents, or 0.57%, to $86.53.

New data showed that 37 ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and ​surrounding waterways in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, ​according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. And 10 attacks ⁠have been recorded so far in November.

Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified ​by Reuters showed a Navig8 tanker on fire near the coast of Oman, one of three ​tankers hit on Sunday for using “unauthorised routes” through the strait, according to the Iranian state broadcaster.

Another tanker was struck northeast of Oman’s Lima, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday.

Iran’s Revolutionary ​Guards Navy said in a separate statement on Tuesday that two tankers caught fire after ​hitting naval mines on the “unauthorised route” in the strait.

“Even in the event a deal is struck, an increase ‌in ⁠flows through the waterway would still depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and whether or not shipowners would even be willing to take the risk,” LSEG analysts said in a November 10 note. “Meanwhile, attacks have not slowed.”

In the previous session, oil prices initially fell by more than $3 a ​barrel after US officials downplayed ​the need for further ⁠military strikes against Iran, but then gained back some of those losses after an Iranian security official said no talks were taking place between ​the two sides.

US crude oil stocks rose in the latest week, market ​sources said, ⁠citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks rose by 9 million barrels in the week ended November 6, the sources said.

In Russia, oil refining capacity has been reduced by about 30% since ⁠late ​October following renewed Ukrainian drone attacks, industry sources said.

Russian and ​Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first peace talks since February as US President Donald Trump’s ​envoys launched a fresh push to end the war.

headline: Shehbaz to highlight Pakistan's climate priorities at COP31 summit
description: PM will call for stronger global climate action and cooperation in his address in Antalya
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is scheduled to address the Leaders’ Summit of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in Antalya on Wednesday.

In his speech, the prime minister will highlight Pakistan’s climate priorities and emphasise the urgent need for enhanced global climate action and strengthened international cooperation to mitigate the adverse impacts of climate change, in accordance with established principles.

The prime minister will also address the High-Level Dialogue on Clean Energy Transition and Electrification, titled “35 by 35: Powering the Future.”

On the sidelines of the Summit, the prime minister is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with Turkish President Recep Erdogan and other world leaders attending COP31 to discuss matters of mutual interest and strengthen bilateral cooperation.

A “Pakistan Pavilion” has been established at the COP31 venue, where 54 events will be hosted on various themes.

Pakistan’s contributions in previous COP outcomes include active climate diplomacy that led to the establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund during COP27.

Earlier, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif arrived in Antalya, Türkiye, on an official visit.

Upon arrival, the prime minister was received by Turkey’s Deputy Minister of Culture and Tourism Gökhan Yazgi, Pakistan’s Ambassador-designate to Türkiye Amna Baloch, and senior Turkish officials, a press release issued by the Prime Minister’s Office said.

headline: Cooking on wood, skipping meals: Bangladesh workers battle rising costs
description: Workers say their factory wages are no longer enough to feed their families, prompting protests
author: Reuters
article_text:
Before dawn ​each day, garment worker Shilpi Khatun cooks over a wood-fired clay stove because her family cannot afford gas, before ‌heading to a factory in Gazipur, an industrial hub on the outskirts of Dhaka.

The 27-year-old is the sole breadwinner in a household where her husband is unemployed, and her parents and in-laws depend on her wages.

Rising prices have left Khatun struggling to afford necessities despite five years in the garment industry, a frustration ​shared by thousands of Bangladesh’s garment workers who staged protests last week demanding the minimum monthly wage be raised to 30,000 ​taka ($242.82) from 12,500 taka.

“Everything costs more now. Rent has doubled, food is more expensive and whatever I earn ⁠disappears before the month is over,” Khatun said as she gathered leafy greens outside her home to eat with rice for lunch.

Wage pressure mounts

Last week’s unrest, some of it violent, forced hundreds of factories to shut down as workers staged protests and clashed with police, who used tear ​gas and sound grenades to disperse demonstrators.

The government’s wage board agreed on November 4 to implement a revised wage structure from December, with workers set to receive their first pay under the new scale in January, but it has yet to determine the size of the increase.

Low labour costs have helped make Bangladesh the ​world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China and a preferred manufacturing base for global brands including H&M, Zara, Gap, Primark and Walmart.

The industry ​generates more than 80% of the country’s export earnings and employs more than 4 million people.

Manufacturers, however, say a steep wage increase would erode Bangladesh’s cost ‌advantage over ⁠rivals such as India and Vietnam and further squeeze margins already under pressure from higher energy costs.

Workers also receive a 9% annual increment and two festival bonuses in addition to their basic wages, manufacturers say, arguing there is limited room for substantial pay increases.

Workers make stark choices

Workers like Khatun say the wage increase has not kept pace with rising prices, forcing them to make difficult choices over everyday spending.

On the hardest ​days, Khatun’s family survives on puffed ​rice, she said. Sitting in ⁠the small tin-shed room she shares with her husband, she said she had not seen a doctor in three years despite worsening health problems.

Her salary has crept up over five years but not enough to ​match rising costs. She now earns 13,500 taka ($108), up from 9,000 taka when she started.

With overtime, ​she earns about ⁠16,000 taka, but the money rarely lasts until the next payday, she said.

Bangladesh has faced a prolonged cost-of-living squeeze since 2022, with inflation averaging around 9%. Food prices initially drove the surge, but non-food costs have remained high.

“I think twice before buying anything, even food,” said Roksana Parveen, a 29-year ⁠old sewing ​operator in a factory in Ashulia on the outskirts of Dhaka.

“I know my daughters ​should be eating better, but I just can’t afford it.”

Parveen and her two daughters often live on little more than rice and vegetables, with meat and fish becoming luxuries ​beyond their reach. To cut costs, one of her daughters dropped out of school.

headline: US judge says Trump’s $10 billion BBC defamation case can proceed
description: US judge allows defamation claim but dismisses unfair trade practices charge
author: Reuters
article_text:
A federal judge on Tuesday said President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC over a misleadingly ​edited clip of a speech can go forward, but threw out ‌Trump’s unfair trade practices claim against the broadcaster.

Trump is suing Britain’s publicly funded broadcaster for at least $10 billion over edited clips of a speech that made it appear he directed supporters ​to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.

The case is ​one of several Trump has filed against the news media as ⁠part of a wider pressure campaign against coverage he dislikes.

US District Judge ​Jeffrey Kuntz in Florida declined to throw out Trump’s defamation claim against the BBC, ​saying Trump had plausibly alleged that the broadcaster damaged his reputation and knew or should have known the clip was misleading. Kuntz’s ruling did not decide whether Trump has proven those ​claims.

Trump called the ruling a “huge victory” in a social media post. “We will continue ​fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” he ‌wrote.

A ⁠BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster was surprised by the decision but respects the court’s authority and remains confident in its position.

The BBC has previously admitted the edits were misleading and apologized to Trump, though it denies being liable for defamation.

Trump’s lawsuit, ​filed in December ​in Florida federal ⁠court, accuses the BBC of defaming him by splicing together parts of the speech, including one section where he told supporters ​to march on the Capitol and another where he said “fight ​like hell”. ⁠It omitted a section in which he called for peaceful protest.

The edited speech appeared in a BBC “Panorama” documentary show shortly before the 2024 presidential election, which Trump won.

⁠A ​leaked internal BBC memo cited the edits as ​evidence of potential political bias, sparking a public relations crisis for the broadcaster and leading to high-level ​resignations.

headline: Missing sailors leave families desperate for answers after Iran war
description: Families fear for crew members missing near Strait of Hormuz
author: Reuters
article_text:
V. Pandiselvi, the mother of Indian sailor Naveen Kumar, has not heard from her son for more than six months, yet she still clings to the hope that he will return, crying as ​she replays old voice notes.

Kumar was one of six crew members assigned to work on two Iran-linked cargo vessels last seen in Iranian waters in May before disappearing. The vessels’ fate is still unclear.

Commercial ships ‌have come under fire since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28.

Tehran attacked ships to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, and the US, in turn, struck Iran-linked ships to impose a blockade on Iranian ports.

The UN’s International Maritime Organisation has confirmed 130 “incidents” – mainly attacks – in the region since the conflict began, with at least 25 seafarers killed.

“We cannot bear this pain,” Pandiselvi, 45, told Reuters from her one-bedroom house in the city of Dindigul in southern India’s Tamil Nadu state, struggling to keep her composure.

“You don’t need anyone to tell you what a parent would go through if they ​were to lose their child. We appeal to everyone involved to please come forward and help us.”

Reuters spoke to shipping sources, Iraqi officials and the families of missing sailors in Iraq’s Basra and India’s Tamil Nadu state to reveal ​the human cost of Hormuz attacks.

The 23-year-old Kumar’s family took on considerable debt for him to complete a marine course and pursue his dream of working as a sailor, after which he ⁠left for a six-month crew contract he was told was based in Dubai. A week in, he found himself in Iran, to the consternation of his family.

‘Every minute is agony’

Even before war broke out three months later, Kumar’s family was desperately trying to ​repatriate him. Then came radio silence.

“My mental condition had deteriorated into madness; I sent desperate messages,” Pandiselvi said, adding she was sending him voice notes without any replies to a number she had saved as “Naveen Mariner” with an anchor emoji.

The family keeps the line ​active in the hope their son picks up. A neighbour described her as listening to messages over and over, in tears.

“A terrifying question mark hangs over his fate: Is he still on that ship, or has something terrible happened to him? It’s causing a lot of confusion. Every passing minute is agony,” Pandiselvi said.

Kumar had been deployed to the vessels Bridge 1 and Bridge 2, which disappeared around May 9. The two ships were not on the IMO’s list of incidents.

Iraq said in May it was monitoring the disappearance of the two vessels, which flew the Bolivian flag. No distress signals ​were received. Gulf ports requested information after communications with the crew were lost.

Khaled Saad al-Thaalibi, who heads the Iraqi maritime foundation in Basra, told Reuters the latest available information indicated the vessels’ Automatic Identification System (AIS) transmitted their last known position approximately 8 nautical miles ​from Iran’s Kish Island on May 9 at 4:50pm.

“We called the agent in Iran, but he told us that he knew nothing about the incident and on the following day the Iranian search and rescue tried to look for the vessels, but they found nothing,” Thaalibi ‌told Reuters from ⁠his office in Basra.

“We don’t know if the vessels sank or were confiscated by a country.”

The other Bridge 1 and 2 crew members missing are three Iraqis, one Pakistani and another Indian.

Sources familiar with the matter said the vessels were involved in Iranian trade and were carrying steel.

No answers

Haider Rahman al-Mayahi, a 22-year-old Iraqi sailor, was on the crew, his brother Youssef Rahman said.

“He left behind a one-year-old daughter and a father who suffered a stroke from the grief of his disappearance,” he told Reuters, breaking down in tears.

Al-Mayahi’s family travelled to Iran seeking answers. They located the vessels’ owner, whom they identified only as an Iranian who told them he had no information on the vessels.

The family received conflicting theories about the vessels.

Some shipping sources said they may have been struck by the ​US and sunk immediately, while others speculated the crew had ​been detained by a Gulf state or Iran.

The Iranian agent ⁠who hired the Iraqi sailors did not respond to phone calls from Reuters.

Kumar’s family took out around 1.5 million Indian rupees ($16,000) in loans for him to complete his maritime training course and is now struggling with the financial burden.

They contacted the local agency that hired Kumar, Mumbai-based firm Lascar Marine, initially receiving assurances that he would return soon.

People from the agency later told the family they ​had no information. After that, calls went unanswered, the family said.

The agency did not reply to repeated calls from Reuters.

An order dated May 22, published on a government website, showed ​India’s Seamen’s Employment Office withdrew the recruitment ⁠license of Lascar Marine Services and barred its past and present directors from maritime business for five years, citing repeated failures to repatriate seafarers — including Kumar — or pay their wages.

The director of Seamen’s Employment Office did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Crew working aboard ships are usually contracted by agents like Lascar Marine and hired on six-month contracts. Since the Iran war, costs of hiring sailors have tripled, with many working just one journey as risks mount.

One Dubai-based shipper told Reuters a crew member may make what they used to make ⁠in seven months ​in only two and then opt to go home.

A captain, the highest-paid crew member on a vessel, could make around $8,000 to $13,000 a month before ​the conflict. Now they can earn three times that.

“They ask for three months’ pay per month, but after seeing what a journey entails, they sometimes quit after one trip,” the shipper said.

For Pandiselvi, Kumar’s mother, the allure of good pay is now meaningless.

“We worked tirelessly to secure our children’s careers and future,” she said. “Now, ​seeing everything that has happened, we are left wondering what our lives have come to.”

Kumar was one of six crew members assigned to work on two Iran-linked cargo vessels last seen in Iranian waters in May before disappearing. The vessels’ fate is still unclear.
Commercial ships ‌have come under fire since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28.
Tehran attacked ships to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, and the US, in turn, struck Iran-linked ships to impose a blockade on Iranian ports.
The UN’s International Maritime Organisation has confirmed 130 “incidents” – mainly attacks – in the region since the conflict began, with at least 25 seafarers killed.
“We cannot bear this pain,” Pandiselvi, 45, told Reuters from her one-bedroom house in the city of Dindigul in southern India’s Tamil Nadu state, struggling to keep her composure.
“You don’t need anyone to tell you what a parent would go through if they were to lose their child. We appeal to everyone involved to please come forward and help us.”
Reuters spoke to shipping sources, Iraqi officials and the families of missing sailors in Iraq’s Basra and India’s Tamil Nadu state to reveal the human cost of Hormuz attacks.

The 23-year-old Kumar’s family took on considerable debt for him to complete a marine course and pursue his dream of working as a sailor, after which he ⁠left for a six-month crew contract he was told was based in Dubai. A week in, he found himself in Iran, to the consternation of his family.
‘Every minute is agony’
Even before war broke out three months later, Kumar’s family was desperately trying to repatriate him. Then came radio silence.

“My mental condition had deteriorated into madness; I sent desperate messages,” Pandiselvi said, adding she was sending him voice notes without any replies to a number she had saved as “Naveen Mariner” with an anchor emoji.
The family keeps the line active in the hope their son picks up. A neighbour described her as listening to messages over and over, in tears.
“A terrifying question mark hangs over his fate: Is he still on that ship, or has something terrible happened to him? It’s causing a lot of confusion. Every passing minute is agony,” Pandiselvi said.
Kumar had been deployed to the vessels Bridge 1 and Bridge 2, which disappeared around May 9. The two ships were not on the IMO’s list of incidents.

Iraq said in May it was monitoring the disappearance of the two vessels, which flew the Bolivian flag. No distress signals were received. Gulf ports requested information after communications with the crew were lost.

Khaled Saad al-Thaalibi, who heads the Iraqi maritime foundation in Basra, told Reuters the latest available information indicated the vessels’ Automatic Identification System (AIS) transmitted their last known position approximately 8 nautical miles from Iran’s Kish Island on May 9 at 4:50pm.

“We called the agent in Iran, but he told us that he knew nothing about the incident and on the following day the Iranian search and rescue tried to look for the vessels, but they found nothing,” Thaalibi ‌told Reuters from ⁠his office in Basra.
“We don’t know if the vessels sank or were confiscated by a country.”
The other Bridge 1 and 2 crew members missing are three Iraqis, one Pakistani and another Indian.
Sources familiar with the matter said the vessels were involved in Iranian trade and were carrying steel.
No answers
Haider Rahman al-Mayahi, a 22-year-old Iraqi sailor, was on the crew, his brother Youssef Rahman said.
“He left behind a one-year-old daughter and a father who suffered a stroke from the grief of his disappearance,” he told Reuters, breaking down in tears.
Al-Mayahi’s family travelled to Iran seeking answers. They located the vessels’ owner, whom they identified only as an Iranian who told them he had no information on the vessels.
The family received conflicting theories about the vessels.
Some shipping sources said they may have been struck by the US and sunk immediately, while others speculated the crew had been detained by a Gulf state or Iran.
The Iranian agent ⁠who hired the Iraqi sailors did not respond to phone calls from Reuters.
Kumar’s family took out around 1.5 million Indian rupees ($16,000) in loans for him to complete his maritime training course and is now struggling with the financial burden.
They contacted the local agency that hired Kumar, Mumbai-based firm Lascar Marine, initially receiving assurances that he would return soon.
People from the agency later told the family they had no information. After that, calls went unanswered, the family said.
The agency did not reply to repeated calls from Reuters.

An order dated May 22, published on a government website, showed India’s Seamen’s Employment Office withdrew the recruitment ⁠license of Lascar Marine Services and barred its past and present directors from maritime business for five years, citing repeated failures to repatriate seafarers — including Kumar — or pay their wages.
The director of Seamen’s Employment Office did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Crew working aboard ships are usually contracted by agents like Lascar Marine and hired on six-month contracts. Since the Iran war, costs of hiring sailors have tripled, with many working just one journey as risks mount.
One Dubai-based shipper told Reuters a crew member may make what they used to make ⁠in seven months in only two and then opt to go home.
A captain, the highest-paid crew member on a vessel, could make around $8,000 to $13,000 a month before the conflict. Now they can earn three times that.
“They ask for three months’ pay per month, but after seeing what a journey entails, they sometimes quit after one trip,” the shipper said.
For Pandiselvi, Kumar’s mother, the allure of good pay is now meaningless.
“We worked tirelessly to secure our children’s careers and future,” she said. “Now, seeing everything that has happened, we are left wondering what our lives have come to.”

headline: No evidence of domestic discord in slain TV anchor's phone chats
description: Police send mobile phones of Rabia Ahsan and her husband for forensic analysis
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The Rawalpindi Police investigating the murder of TV anchor Rabia Ahsan have found no evidence of a domestic dispute or discord in the chat records exchanged between the victim and her husband, Ahsan, the suspect, sources said on Wednesday.

The investigation team has sent both mobile phones to a forensic laboratory for further analysis and collection of evidence.

Rabia was shot dead at her residence in the Gulshanabad area of Rawalpindi on November 8.

Meanwhile, police have taken the suspect to Lahore for a polygraph test as part of the ongoing investigation during his physical remand, the sources said.

The police team has also taken samples collected during the post-mortem examination to Lahore for forensic analysis at the Punjab Forensic Science Laboratory.

According to the sources, the suspect will also undergo a DNA test in Lahore.

Investigators are continuing to question the suspect and record statements from the victim’s family as they pursue different aspects of the case, the sources added.

headline: Baby boy found alive in US after believed buried for 24 hours, police say
description: Infant was discovered inside a dog crate after a day-long search in South Carolina
author: Reuters
article_text:
An 11-month-old boy was found alive in South Carolina on Tuesday after he ​was believed to have been buried for ‌about 24 hours, the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department said.

The infant, Koah Sharpe, was found wrapped in a towel in ​a dog crate, shallowly buried in the woods, ​according to the department.

“Certainly God is good. Just ⁠a few moments ago, we found little ​Koah, 11 months old, buried alive, clinging to life, ​crying — the most joyful sound you ever heard of a crying baby,” Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said during a ​news conference.

Koon said the infant’s father, Michael ​Comer, was arrested on Monday night on burglary and resisting arrest. ‌

The ⁠department is working with the solicitor’s office to determine additional charges, he said.

Koah went missing on Monday after being left in his father’s care ​at his mother’s ​home while ⁠she ran an errand, Koon said.

The boy was reported missing, and ​authorities began a widespread search, according to ​the ⁠sheriff.

Koah was found after a search party discovered “freshly disturbed” dirt in the woods about 50 yards from ⁠Comer’s ​father’s house, Koon said.

The infant ​is currently at the hospital and will “hopefully” recover, the sheriff said.

headline: Imran Khan's health stable, vital signs normal, says PIMS
description: Ex-PM was administered an anti-VEGF injection in his eye during a late-night visit to PIMS
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder Imran Khan was taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad from Adiala jail late Tuesday night for a medical examination, jail sources said on Wednesday.

A special team of doctors conducted a detailed medical check-up of the former prime minister, including examinations of his blood pressure, temperature and eyes, according to the sources.

After the examination and necessary medical tests were completed, Imran Khan was transferred back to Adiala jail under tight security arrangements.

The latest medical examination comes days after Khan was examined at the jail on November 8.

PIMS issues statement

Meanwhile, the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) has issued a statement on the medical examination of PTI founder Imran Khan, saying all his vital signs were found normal and his overall physical condition was satisfactory and stable.

According to the hospital administration, Khan was shifted from Adiala jail to PIMS late at night and brought to the hospital during the night between November 10 and 11 for a medical examination.

He underwent a general medical check-up as well as follow-up treatment for his eyes, the statement said.

The former premier stayed at the hospital for 40-50 minutes for the medical examination, PIMS said.

It added that, on the recommendation of an eye specialist, Khan was administered an anti-VEGF injection in his eye. The procedure was carried out by the hospital’s ophthalmology team.

The hospital said his vital signs remained within the normal range during the examination, and his overall physical condition was found to be satisfactory and stable.

headline: Jamie Campbell Bower calls Rings of Power role a childhood dream
description: Fantasy series returns with its third season on Prime Video
author: Reuters
article_text:
British actor Jamie Campbell ​Bower said joining “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” fulfilled a childhood dream as the ‌cast gathered in London for the global premiere of the fantasy series’ third season on Tuesday.

Speaking to Reuters, the “Stranger Things” and “Harry Potter” star recalled receiving the email offering him a role in the series.

“It felt like home. It felt very warm and loving,” he said. “Of course, there’s the inner ​child in me who watched the films growing up, who’s screaming.”

The new season jumps forward five years after the ​events of season two and thrusts viewers into the heart of Sauron’s war against the Elves.

Co-showrunner ⁠J.D. Payne said the first two seasons focused on introducing audiences to key characters and storylines across Middle-earth before bringing them ​together in season three.

“All roads lead to Sauron this season,” Payne said. “He’s forging the One Ring, and as a fan, seeing ​the volcano, seeing Charlie Vickers there with the hammer … it’s a really, really special moment.”

Vickers, who plays the antagonist Sauron in the series, said filming the forging scenes was physically demanding.

“It took a lot out of us. But then you just have to pinch yourself and be like, what an ​incredible job and incredible thing to be a part of,” Vickers said.

One of television’s most expensive productions, “The Rings of Power” is ​known for its expansive sets and large-scale world-building.

Welsh actor Morfydd Clark, who plays Elven commander Galadriel, said the number of people involved in bringing ‌the fantasy ⁠world to life often goes unnoticed.

“It’s a whole village,” she said. “If you don’t know what to do when you’re leaving school, look into the types of things that are needed on a film set. You will find the perfect thing for you.”

But for actor Cynthia Addai-Robinson, the enduring appeal of the series lies not in its battles or visual spectacle, but in the relationships ​at its heart.

“I think what ​keeps an audience engaged and ⁠coming back is the relationship between brother and sister, father and daughter, best friends, lovers. Even though it’s fantasy, it feels very humanistic.”

The series has also resonated beyond the screen since its ​debut in 2022.

Actor Ismael Cruz Cordova reflected on the role “The Rings of Power” has played ​in wider conversations ⁠about diversity, representation and fandom.

The Puerto Rican actor was among cast members who faced online backlash because of the colour of his skin when the show first launched.

Cruz Cordova said he feels the discussion has now moved beyond those criticisms.

“The focus has shifted to how impactful ​it has been and how real this character has been able to touch ​people’s lives.”

“I belong everywhere, and we belong everywhere. And no one should feel like they should be limited for any reason whatsoever to dream and to ​actually achieve it.”

The first four episodes of season three will be released on Prime Video on Wednesday.

article_html:
British actor Jamie Campbell ​Bower said joining “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” fulfilled a childhood dream as the ‌cast gathered in London for the global premiere of the fantasy series’ third season on Tuesday.

Speaking to Reuters, the “Stranger Things” and “Harry Potter” star recalled receiving the email offering him a role in the series.

“It felt like home. It felt very warm and loving,” he said. “Of course, there’s the inner ​child in me who watched the films growing up, who’s screaming.”

The new season jumps forward five years after the ​events of season two and thrusts viewers into the heart of Sauron’s war against the Elves.

Co-showrunner ⁠J.D. Payne said the first two seasons focused on introducing audiences to key characters and storylines across Middle-earth before bringing them ​together in season three.

“All roads lead to Sauron this season,” Payne said. “He’s forging the One Ring, and as a fan, seeing ​the volcano, seeing Charlie Vickers there with the hammer … it’s a really, really special moment.”

Vickers, who plays the antagonist Sauron in the series, said filming the forging scenes was physically demanding.

“It took a lot out of us. But then you just have to pinch yourself and be like, what an ​incredible job and incredible thing to be a part of,” Vickers said.

One of television’s most expensive productions, “The Rings of Power” is ​known for its expansive sets and large-scale world-building.

Welsh actor Morfydd Clark, who plays Elven commander Galadriel, said the number of people involved in bringing ‌the fantasy ⁠world to life often goes unnoticed.

“It’s a whole village,” she said. “If you don’t know what to do when you’re leaving school, look into the types of things that are needed on a film set. You will find the perfect thing for you.”

But for actor Cynthia Addai-Robinson, the enduring appeal of the series lies not in its battles or visual spectacle, but in the relationships ​at its heart.

“I think what ​keeps an audience engaged and ⁠coming back is the relationship between brother and sister, father and daughter, best friends, lovers. Even though it’s fantasy, it feels very humanistic.”

The series has also resonated beyond the screen since its ​debut in 2022.

Actor Ismael Cruz Cordova reflected on the role “The Rings of Power” has played ​in wider conversations ⁠about diversity, representation and fandom.

The Puerto Rican actor was among cast members who faced online backlash because of the colour of his skin when the show first launched.

Cruz Cordova said he feels the discussion has now moved beyond those criticisms.

“The focus has shifted to how impactful ​it has been and how real this character has been able to touch ​people’s lives.”

“I belong everywhere, and we belong everywhere. And no one should feel like they should be limited for any reason whatsoever to dream and to ​actually achieve it.”

The first four episodes of season three will be released on Prime Video on Wednesday.
